meta.name: AI Glossary
meta.description: Core AI terms with one-line definitions. Scoped to established, widely used terminology; not exhaustive.

terms.definition: The field of building computer systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as reasoning, perception, and language.
terms.mental_model: A toolbox of techniques for making computers do things we used to think needed a human brain.
terms.example: Google Maps rerouting you around a traffic jam it predicted from live data.

quiz.question: Which of these is the best description of AI?
options: Computer systems that perform tasks normally needing human intelligence
A programming language for data science
A robot with a human-like body
Any software that runs on the internet
quiz.explanation: AI is a broad field defined by the kind of task, not by robots or a specific language.

terms.definition: A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules.
terms.mental_model: Instead of writing the rules, you show the computer examples and it works out the rules itself.
terms.example: Gmail's spam filter learning what spam looks like from millions of emails people marked as spam.

quiz.question: What makes machine learning different from traditional programming?
options: It doesn't need any data
It learns patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules
It never makes mistakes
It only runs on GPUs
quiz.explanation: ML systems derive their behavior from examples; traditional programs follow rules a developer wrote.

terms.definition: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers to learn complex patterns from large amounts of data.
terms.mental_model: Machine learning with many stacked layers, where each layer learns a slightly more abstract pattern than the last.
terms.example: Face ID recognizing your face in different lighting and angles.

quiz.question: What does the 'deep' in deep learning refer to?
options: How long training takes
How complex the answers are
The many layers in the neural network
How much data the model reads
quiz.explanation: Deep refers to the number of layers in the network.

terms.definition: A model made of layers of connected nodes (neurons) whose weighted connections are adjusted during training to map inputs to outputs.
terms.mental_model: A huge web of adjustable dials; training turns the dials until the right inputs produce the right outputs.
terms.example: A network that looks at a photo's pixels and outputs 'cat' with 97% confidence.

quiz.question: What gets adjusted when a neural network is trained?
options: The number of users
The input data
The computer's hardware
The weights on the connections between neurons
quiz.explanation: Training changes the connection weights so the network's outputs get closer to the correct answers.

terms.definition: AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code based on patterns learned from training data.
terms.mental_model: AI that makes new things in the style of what it learned from, instead of only sorting or labeling existing things.
terms.example: Asking an image model for 'a coffee shop logo in a minimalist style' and getting four new designs.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of generative AI?
options: A database search
A model that writes a product description from a short prompt
A model that labels an email as spam or not spam
A calculator app
quiz.explanation: Generative AI produces new content; a spam classifier only assigns a label.

terms.definition: AI designed to perform a specific task or limited set of tasks, which describes nearly all AI in use today.
A hypothetical AI able to match or exceed human ability across most cognitive tasks; there is no agreed definition or test for it.
A hypothetical AI whose intelligence greatly surpasses the best human minds across virtually all domains.
A defined sequence of steps a computer follows to solve a problem or perform a computation.
The trained mathematical system, defined by its architecture and learned parameters, that turns inputs into predictions or outputs.
terms.mental_model: The finished 'brain' that comes out of training: a file of numbers plus the structure that uses them.
terms.example: Downloading an open-weight model file and running it on your own laptop.

quiz.question: What is an AI model, in practical terms?
options: A trained system of architecture plus learned parameters that turns inputs into outputs
A website where you chat with AI
A type of computer chip
The dataset used for training
quiz.explanation: The model is the trained artifact; the chat website is just one app built on top of it.

terms.definition: The numerical values inside a model, learned during training, that determine how it transforms inputs into outputs.
terms.mental_model: The knobs inside a model; training sets their values, and together they store everything the model learned.
terms.example: A '70B' model has about 70 billion of these learned numbers.

quiz.question: What does '8B' usually mean in a model's name?
options: It has about 8 billion parameters
It was trained for 8 billion seconds
It knows 8 billion facts
It costs 8 billion dollars
quiz.explanation: The number in a model name usually refers to its parameter count.

terms.definition: Running a trained model on new input to produce an output, as opposed to training it.
terms.mental_model: Training is studying; inference is taking the exam: the model uses what it learned, without learning anything new.
terms.example: Every time you send a message to a chatbot and it replies, that reply is an inference.

quiz.question: Which of these is inference?
options: A trained model answering a user's question
Adjusting a model's weights
Collecting data to train a model
Choosing a model's architecture
quiz.explanation: Inference is running an already-trained model on new input.

terms.definition: The process of adjusting a model's parameters using data so its outputs become more accurate.
terms.mental_model: Practice with an answer key: the model guesses, checks how wrong it was, and nudges its knobs to do better next time.
terms.example: An AI lab running thousands of GPUs for weeks to train a new language model on internet text.

quiz.question: What happens to a model during training?
options: It gets connected to the internet
Users chat with it for the first time
It is compressed to a smaller file
Its parameters are adjusted using data to reduce errors
quiz.explanation: Training updates the model's parameters; using the model afterward is called inference.

terms.definition: An approach to AI that uses explicit, human-written rules and logic rather than learning from data.
A rule-based program that encodes a human expert's knowledge to make decisions in a narrow domain.
Training a model on labeled examples so it learns to predict the correct label for new inputs.
terms.mental_model: Learning with a teacher who marks every answer right or wrong.
terms.example: Training a model on 10,000 house listings with their sale prices so it can predict prices of new listings.

quiz.question: What does supervised learning need that unsupervised learning doesn't?
options: A language model
A GPU
An internet connection
Labeled examples with the correct answers
quiz.explanation: Supervised learning learns from input-label pairs; unsupervised learning works without labels.

terms.definition: Training a model on unlabeled data so it discovers structure, such as groups or patterns, on its own.
Learning where labels are generated from the data itself, such as predicting the next word, enabling training on huge unlabeled datasets.
Training that combines a small amount of labeled data with a large amount of unlabeled data.
Learning where an agent takes actions in an environment and improves by maximizing reward signals over time.
A task where the model assigns an input to one of a set of predefined categories.
A task where the model predicts a continuous numerical value, such as a price or temperature.
Grouping data points so that items in the same group are more similar to each other than to items in other groups.
A measurable input property or variable that a model uses to make predictions.
The correct answer attached to a training example, which the model learns to predict.
When a model memorizes training data, including its noise, and performs poorly on new, unseen data.
terms.mental_model: A student who memorizes last year's exam answers and fails when the questions change.
terms.example: A model scoring 99% on training data but 60% on new customer data.

quiz.question: Which sign points to overfitting?
options: High accuracy on training data but much lower on new data
Equal accuracy everywhere
The model trains faster than expected
Low accuracy on both training and test data
quiz.explanation: A large gap between training and test performance means the model memorized rather than generalized.

terms.definition: When a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns, performing poorly even on training data.
A model's ability to perform well on new data it did not see during training.
The balance between errors from overly simple assumptions (bias) and errors from oversensitivity to training data (variance).
A formula that measures how far a model's predictions are from the correct answers, which training tries to minimize.
An optimization method that repeatedly adjusts parameters in the direction that most reduces the loss.
A setting that controls how large each parameter update is during training.
A configuration value set before training, such as learning rate or batch size, rather than learned from data.
One complete pass through the entire training dataset.
The number of training examples processed together before the model's parameters are updated once.
Techniques that discourage overly complex models to reduce overfitting.
Evaluating a model by repeatedly training and testing on different splits of the data to estimate how well it generalizes.
Dividing data into separate sets for training, tuning, and final evaluation so performance is measured on unseen data.
A model that makes predictions by following a tree of if-then splits on feature values.
An ensemble of many decision trees trained on random data subsets whose predictions are combined.
An ensemble method that builds models one after another, each correcting the errors of the previous ones.
A model that predicts a numeric value as a weighted sum of input features.
A model that predicts the probability of a binary outcome using a weighted sum of features passed through a sigmoid function.
A classifier that finds the boundary separating classes with the widest possible margin.
A clustering algorithm that splits data into K groups by assigning each point to the nearest group center.
A method that predicts based on the labels of the K most similar examples in the training data.
Combining multiple models so their joint prediction is more accurate than any single one.
Reducing the number of input variables while preserving the most important information, often using methods like PCA.
Identifying data points that deviate significantly from normal patterns.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task.
Training a shared model across many devices or servers without moving the raw data to a central location.
A training approach where the model selects which unlabeled examples a human should label next to learn most efficiently.
Updating a model continuously as new data arrives rather than training once on a fixed dataset.
Learning new tasks over time without forgetting previously learned ones.
When a model loses previously learned knowledge after being trained on new data.
A basic unit in a neural network that computes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies an activation function.
A group of neurons that processes input together and passes its output to the next stage of the network.
A nonlinear function applied to a neuron's output that lets networks learn complex, nonlinear patterns.
The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the error so gradients can be used to update them.
A neural network that uses convolution filters to detect spatial patterns, widely used for images.
A neural network that processes sequences step by step while carrying a hidden state from previous steps.
A type of RNN with gates that control what to remember or forget, helping it handle longer sequences.
A neural network architecture built on attention that processes all tokens in parallel and underlies most modern language models.
A mechanism that lets a model weigh how relevant each part of the input is when processing another part.
Attention in which each token in a sequence computes relevance scores against every other token in the same sequence.
Running several attention operations in parallel so the model can track different kinds of relationships at once.
The part of a model that converts input into an internal representation capturing its meaning.
The part of a model that generates output step by step from an internal representation.
A network trained to compress input into a smaller representation and then reconstruct it.
An autoencoder that learns a probability distribution over its compressed space, allowing it to generate new samples.
Two networks trained against each other, a generator that creates fakes and a discriminator that tries to spot them.
A regularization technique that randomly disables neurons during training to reduce overfitting.
Rescaling activations inside a network to stabilize and speed up training.
A shortcut that adds a layer's input to its output, making very deep networks easier to train.
Information added to token representations so a transformer knows the order of tokens in a sequence.
An architecture where a router activates only a few specialized sub-networks per token, so total parameters can grow without matching compute cost.
A sequence architecture that processes long inputs in linear time by maintaining a compact evolving state, an alternative to attention.
A training problem where gradients become too small in early layers for those layers to learn effectively.
The field of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, process, and generate human language.
A model that assigns probabilities to sequences of text, typically by predicting the next token.
A very large transformer-based language model trained on massive text data that can generate and understand language across many tasks.
terms.mental_model: An extremely well-read autocomplete that has learned language so deeply it can write, summarize, translate, and reason.
terms.example: Claude, GPT and Gemini drafting an email reply from a few bullet points.

quiz.question: At its core, what does an LLM do when generating text?
options: Predicts the next token, over and over
Looks the answer up in a database
Copies text from websites in real time
Runs a fixed script of responses
quiz.explanation: LLMs generate text one token at a time, each predicted from the tokens before it.

terms.definition: A compact language model with relatively few parameters, designed to run cheaply or on-device for focused tasks.
A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
One of the most capable AI models available at a given time, typically from leading labs.
A decoder-only transformer architecture pretrained to predict the next token, and the name of OpenAI's model family.
A chunk of text, such as a word or word piece, that a language model reads and generates as its basic unit.
terms.mental_model: The Lego bricks of text: a model reads and writes in word pieces, not whole words or single letters.
terms.example: 'unbelievable' may be split into tokens like 'un', 'believ' and 'able'; API pricing is counted per token.

quiz.question: Why do AI APIs charge 'per token'?
options: Tokens are special coins you buy
Tokens are the units the model processes for input and output
Tokens count how many users you have
Each token is one full sentence
quiz.explanation: Models process text as tokens, so cost and limits are measured in them.

terms.definition: Splitting text into tokens the model can process, often using methods like byte-pair encoding.
The fixed set of tokens a model's tokenizer can represent.
Generating text one token at a time, each predicted from all the tokens before it.
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, including both input and output.
terms.mental_model: The model's working desk: everything it can see at once must fit on it, and anything beyond the edge falls off.
terms.example: Pasting a 300-page contract into a chat works only if the model's context window can hold that many tokens.

quiz.question: What happens when a conversation grows larger than the context window?
options: The model gets permanently smarter
The model switches to a bigger model automatically
Older or excess content can no longer be considered
Nothing, context windows are unlimited
quiz.explanation: Only what fits in the context window is visible to the model; the rest must be dropped or summarized.

terms.definition: A list of numbers representing text, images, or other data so that similar meanings sit close together in vector space.
terms.mental_model: GPS coordinates for meaning: similar ideas get nearby coordinates, unrelated ideas end up far apart.
terms.example: 'How do I return a product?' and 'refund policy' get close embeddings, so a help-center search finds the right page.

quiz.question: Why are embeddings useful for search?
options: Texts with similar meaning get similar vectors, so you can find related content
They encrypt the data
They make files smaller
They translate text to English
quiz.explanation: Embeddings let you compare meaning numerically, which powers semantic search and RAG.

terms.definition: The internal multi-dimensional space where a model represents concepts as vectors.
A language model trained to generate intermediate reasoning before answering, improving performance on complex problems.
terms.mental_model: A model that thinks before it speaks, working the problem through in scratch notes first.
terms.example: A reasoning model taking extra seconds to solve a multi-step math or coding problem more reliably.

quiz.question: What is the main trade-off with reasoning models?
options: They never make mistakes
They only work offline
They're often more accurate on hard problems but slower and use more tokens
They can't use language
quiz.explanation: Thinking longer usually costs time and tokens in exchange for better answers on complex tasks.

terms.definition: Extra tokens a model spends working through a problem before giving its final answer.
When a model produces fluent but false or unsupported information presented as fact.
terms.mental_model: A confident student bluffing on an exam: fluent, convincing, and wrong.
terms.example: A chatbot citing a court case with a real-sounding name that never existed.

quiz.question: What is an AI hallucination?
options: When an image model makes blurry pictures
When a model runs out of tokens
When a model states false or made-up information as fact
When a model refuses to answer
quiz.explanation: Hallucinations are plausible but unsupported outputs; grounding with sources like RAG reduces them.

terms.definition: The date after which a model has little or no information because its training data ends there.
terms.mental_model: A history book printed on a certain date: it knows nothing that happened after it went to press.
terms.example: Asking a model about a product launched last month and getting an outdated answer unless it can search the web.

quiz.question: A model with a knowledge cutoff of January 2026 is asked about an event in May 2026. What's most likely?
options: It doesn't know about it unless given search or the information in the prompt
It knows all the details
It automatically retrains
It refuses all questions
quiz.explanation: Models only know their training data; newer information must come from tools or the prompt.

terms.definition: Capabilities that appear in larger models but are absent or weak in smaller ones; whether they are truly sudden is debated.
A model whose trained parameters are publicly released for download and local use, though training data and code may not be.
terms.mental_model: Getting the finished engine to run in your own garage, though not always the factory blueprints.
terms.example: Downloading an open-weight model and running it on your own server so customer data never leaves your machine.

quiz.question: What do you get with an open-weight model?
options: Guaranteed full training data and code
A free cloud subscription
Only API access
The trained parameters to download and run yourself
quiz.explanation: Open-weight releases share the weights; training data and code may still be private.

terms.definition: A model whose weights are not released and is accessed only through the provider's products or API.
Identifying whether text expresses positive, negative, or neutral opinion.
Finding and labeling names of people, places, organizations, and similar entities in text.
Automatically translating text from one language to another.
Producing a shorter version of text that keeps its key information.
The initial large-scale training of a model on broad data to learn general patterns before task-specific adaptation.
All training after pretraining, such as fine-tuning and RLHF, that shapes a model into a useful, safe assistant.
Further training a pretrained model on a smaller, specific dataset to specialize its behavior.
terms.mental_model: Sending a graduate to a specialist course: they keep their general knowledge and get extra skill in one area.
terms.example: Fine-tuning a model on 5,000 past support tickets so it answers in the company's tone and format.

quiz.question: When does fine-tuning usually make more sense than RAG?
options: When you need the model to know facts that change daily
When you want to change the model's style, format or behavior consistently
When you have no data at all
When you want to cite sources
quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning shapes behavior; RAG is better for supplying changing facts.

terms.definition: Fine-tuning on example input-output pairs that demonstrate the desired responses.
Fine-tuning a model on instructions paired with good responses so it follows user requests.
Training a model with a reward signal learned from human ratings of its outputs.
terms.mental_model: Training a dog with treats: people rate answers, and the model learns to give the kind that get good ratings.
terms.example: Human raters ranking several model replies so the model learns to be more helpful and less harmful.

quiz.question: What does the 'HF' in RLHF stand for, and what role does it play?
options: Human Feedback; human preferences become the reward signal
Hardware Filter; it speeds up training
High Frequency; it updates the model hourly
Hidden Function; it hides model weights
quiz.explanation: RLHF uses human preference ratings to train a reward signal that guides the model.

terms.definition: Like RLHF, but the preference feedback comes from an AI model instead of humans.
RL training where rewards come from automatically checkable outcomes, such as correct math answers or passing code tests.
A model trained to score outputs by how well they match human or specified preferences, used to guide RL training.
A method that trains directly on pairs of preferred and rejected responses without a separate reward model.
A reinforcement learning algorithm that improves a policy with limited-size updates for stable training.
An RL method that scores each response relative to a group of sampled responses, avoiding a separate value model.
Anthropic's method of training a model to critique and revise its outputs against a written set of principles.
Fine-tuning methods that update only a small fraction of a model's parameters to cut compute and memory costs.
A PEFT method that trains small low-rank matrices added to frozen model weights.
LoRA applied on top of a quantized base model, making fine-tuning feasible on smaller GPUs.
Training a smaller student model to imitate the outputs of a larger teacher model.
Artificially generated data, often produced by AI models, used for training or testing.
Empirical relationships showing how model performance improves predictably with more parameters, data, and compute.
Improving answer quality by spending more computation during inference, such as longer reasoning or sampling multiple answers.
A saved snapshot of a model's parameters at a point during or after training.
Degradation in quality and diversity when models are trained repeatedly on data generated by other models.
The method used to choose output tokens from a model's predicted probabilities.
A setting that controls randomness in generation; lower values give more predictable output, higher values more varied output.
terms.mental_model: A creativity dial: turn it down for consistent answers, up for more varied and surprising ones.
terms.example: Low temperature for extracting invoice data; higher temperature for brainstorming 20 brand names.

quiz.question: You want the same, predictable answer every time. Which temperature setting fits best?
options: A low temperature
The maximum temperature
A high temperature
Temperature doesn't affect output
quiz.explanation: Lower temperature makes the model favor its most likely tokens, giving more consistent output.

terms.definition: Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose combined probability reaches p.
Sampling only from the k most likely next tokens.
Always choosing the single most likely next token at each step.
Keeping several of the most likely partial sequences at each step and choosing the best complete one.
A limit on how many tokens a model may generate in a single response.
A specified string that makes the model stop generating when it is produced.
Sending a model's output token by token as it is generated instead of waiting for the full response.
The delay between sending a request and receiving output, often measured as time to first token.
How much output a system produces per unit of time, typically tokens per second.
Stored attention keys and values from earlier tokens so they are not recomputed for each new token.
Reusing processed results of a repeated prompt prefix across requests to reduce cost and latency.
Speeding up generation by having a small model draft tokens that the large model then verifies in parallel.
Storing model weights at lower numerical precision, such as 8-bit or 4-bit, to reduce memory and speed up inference.
Removing less important weights or neurons from a model to make it smaller and faster.
Processing many requests together asynchronously, usually at lower cost than real-time calls.
Forcing a model's output to follow a defined format, such as a JSON schema.
The raw scores a model outputs for each possible token before they are converted into probabilities.
A function that converts a list of scores into probabilities that sum to one.
The input text or instructions given to a model to produce a response.
terms.mental_model: The order you give a very capable assistant: the clearer the order, the better the result.
terms.example: 'Summarize this article in 3 bullet points for a busy CEO' is a prompt.

quiz.question: Which prompt will most likely give a better result?
options: 'Write something about marketing'
'Write a 100-word Instagram caption for a Lahore coffee shop's new iced latte, friendly tone'
'Marketing'
'Help'
quiz.explanation: Specific prompts with audience, format and length give the model what it needs.

terms.definition: Designing and refining prompts to get more accurate or useful outputs from a model.
terms.mental_model: Learning how to brief a brilliant new hire who has no context about your situation.
terms.example: Rewriting a vague prompt to include examples, the output format, and the audience until results are consistent.

quiz.question: Which technique is part of prompt engineering?
options: Deleting the context window
Buying more GPUs
Adding examples and a clear output format to the prompt
Retraining the model's weights
quiz.explanation: Prompt engineering improves outputs by changing the input, not the model.

terms.definition: Instructions set by the developer that define a model's role, rules, and behavior for a conversation.
terms.mental_model: The job description handed to the model before the customer walks in.
terms.example: A store's support bot is given 'You are a polite assistant for an online shoe store; only answer questions about orders and returns.'

quiz.question: Who usually writes the system prompt?
options: The internet service provider
The model writes it itself
The end user, in each message
The developer or app builder, to set the model's role and rules
quiz.explanation: Developers set system prompts to define behavior before user messages arrive.

terms.definition: Asking a model to perform a task without giving it any examples.
Including a few input-output examples in the prompt to show the model the desired pattern.
terms.mental_model: Showing someone two finished examples before asking them to do the third.
terms.example: Giving a model three product titles in your store's naming style, then asking it to write a fourth.

quiz.question: What makes a prompt 'few-shot'?
options: It is sent to a few different models
It includes a few examples of the desired input and output
It uses a small model
It is shorter than 10 words
quiz.explanation: Few-shot prompting teaches the pattern through examples placed inside the prompt.

terms.definition: A model's ability to pick up a task from instructions and examples in the prompt without updating its weights.
Having a model write out intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer.
terms.mental_model: Showing your working on a math problem, so mistakes are less likely and easier to spot.
terms.example: Asking 'Think step by step: if a shirt is 2,000 PKR with 15% off, plus 200 delivery, what's the total?'

quiz.question: Why does chain-of-thought often improve answers on complex problems?
options: It makes the model bigger
It lowers the cost
Writing intermediate steps helps the model work through the problem before answering
It connects the model to the internet
quiz.explanation: Reasoning step by step gives the model room to break the problem down instead of jumping to an answer.

terms.definition: Exploring multiple branching reasoning paths and evaluating them to choose the best solution.
Sampling several reasoning paths and picking the most common final answer.
Telling the model to act as a specific role or expert to shape its responses.
Splitting a task into steps where each prompt's output feeds into the next prompt.
A reusable prompt with placeholders that are filled in with specific values at run time.
Deciding what information, tools, memory, and instructions go into a model's limited context window at each step.
Supplying the start of the model's response so it continues in a desired format or direction.
Using a model to write or improve prompts for itself or another model.
Retrieving relevant documents from an external source and adding them to the prompt so the model answers from that information.
terms.mental_model: An open-book exam: before answering, the model is handed the relevant pages to read.
terms.example: A support bot fetching the store's actual return-policy page and answering from it instead of guessing.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of RAG?
options: To generate images
To make the model run faster
To give the model relevant retrieved information so its answers are grounded in real sources
To retrain the model every day
quiz.explanation: RAG adds retrieved documents to the prompt so the model answers from them.

terms.definition: RAG where an agent decides when, where, and how to search, often over multiple rounds, instead of one fixed retrieval step.
RAG that retrieves from a knowledge graph of entities and relationships rather than only text chunks.
A database that stores embeddings and finds the vectors most similar to a query.
terms.mental_model: A library organized by meaning instead of alphabet, so you can ask for 'books like this one'.
terms.example: Storing embeddings of 10,000 help articles so the closest matches to a customer's question can be found in milliseconds.

quiz.question: What does a vector database mainly do?
options: Stores embeddings and finds the most similar ones to a query
Stores passwords
Hosts websites
Trains language models
quiz.explanation: Vector databases are built for fast similarity search over embeddings.

terms.definition: Search that matches by meaning using embeddings rather than exact keywords.
terms.mental_model: Searching by what you mean, not the exact words you typed.
terms.example: Searching 'cheap laptop for students' and finding a page titled 'Budget notebooks for university'.

quiz.question: How is semantic search different from keyword search?
options: It is always slower and less accurate
It matches meaning, so results can match even without the exact words
It requires exact spelling
It only works in English
quiz.explanation: Semantic search compares embeddings, which capture meaning rather than exact wording.

terms.definition: Search that matches exact words, often ranked with algorithms like BM25.
Combining keyword search and semantic search to improve retrieval quality.
Splitting documents into smaller pieces so they can be embedded and retrieved individually.
terms.mental_model: Cutting a long book into index cards, so you can pull out just the card you need.
terms.example: Splitting a 50-page product manual into 300-word sections before embedding it for RAG.

quiz.question: Why are documents chunked before being added to a RAG system?
options: To make them load faster in a browser
So relevant small pieces can be retrieved instead of whole documents
To delete unnecessary words
To translate them
quiz.explanation: Smaller chunks let retrieval return just the relevant passage and fit within the context window.

terms.definition: A measure of how similar two vectors are based on the angle between them.
Fast search methods that find vectors close to a query without checking every vector, trading a little accuracy for speed.
Re-scoring an initial set of retrieved results with a more accurate model to put the most relevant ones first.
Tying a model's answers to specific, verifiable sources or data to reduce hallucination.
terms.mental_model: Making the model show its receipts: every answer should be backed by a source you can check.
terms.example: A legal assistant answering only from the uploaded contract and citing the clause it used.

quiz.question: What is the goal of grounding an AI's answers?
options: To hide where information came from
To make answers longer
To make the model more creative
To tie answers to verifiable sources and reduce hallucinations
quiz.explanation: Grounding links outputs to real data, making them more reliable and checkable.

terms.definition: Linking a generated claim to the specific source passage that supports it.
A curated collection of documents or facts that a system retrieves from.
A structured network of entities and their relationships.
Reformulating a user's question to retrieve better results.
Narrowing retrieval results using attributes like date, category, or author in addition to similarity.
Adding document-level context to each chunk before embedding so chunks remain meaningful when retrieved alone.
An AI system that uses a model to plan and take actions, often with tools, over multiple steps to reach a goal.
terms.mental_model: Moving from a consultant who gives advice to an assistant who actually goes and does the task.
terms.example: An agent that reads your inbox, finds a supplier's invoice, checks it against the order, and drafts a reply.

quiz.question: What best separates an AI agent from a basic chatbot?
options: Agents can plan and take actions with tools across multiple steps
Agents only answer yes or no
Agents never use language models
Agents use bigger fonts
quiz.explanation: Agents act toward a goal using tools in a loop; basic chatbots only reply with text.

terms.definition: AI systems that pursue goals with some autonomy by planning, deciding, and using tools rather than only answering prompts.
The repeated cycle in which an agent reasons, takes an action, observes the result, and decides the next step until done.
A process where an AI decides next steps dynamically rather than following a fixed, scripted sequence.
A model's ability to call external tools, such as search, calculators, or APIs, to get information or take actions.
terms.mental_model: Giving the model hands: it decides which tool to pick up, and your app does the actual work.
terms.example: A model calling a weather API, then using the result to tell you whether to carry an umbrella.

quiz.question: In tool use, who actually runs the tool?
options: The model runs it inside its weights
The user always runs it manually
The application runs it, based on the model's structured request
No one; the result is guessed
quiz.explanation: The model requests a tool call with arguments; the app executes it and returns the result.

terms.definition: A model producing structured arguments for a developer-defined function, which the application then executes.
An open standard, introduced by Anthropic, for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources through a common interface.
terms.mental_model: A USB-C port for AI: one standard plug so any AI app can connect to many tools and data sources.
terms.example: Connecting Claude to Google Drive, Figma or Shopify through MCP servers instead of custom integrations for each.

quiz.question: What problem does MCP solve?
options: It replaces the need for an API key
It compresses models
It makes models smarter by retraining them
It standardizes how AI apps connect to external tools and data
quiz.explanation: MCP gives one common protocol, so integrations don't need to be rebuilt for every app.

terms.definition: An open protocol, introduced by Google, that lets AI agents from different systems communicate and coordinate tasks.
An agent pattern that interleaves reasoning steps with actions and observations.
An agent breaking a goal into ordered subtasks before or while executing them.
Coordinating models, tools, agents, and steps so they work together to complete a task.
Multiple AI agents with separate roles working together or in parallel on a larger task.
An agent launched by a main agent to handle a specific subtask in its own separate context.
The surrounding software that runs a model as an agent, managing its loop, tools, context, and permissions.
Information an agent stores and retrieves across steps or sessions beyond its current context window.
Packaged folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that an agent loads on demand to perform a specialized task.
An agent operating a computer's interface by viewing screenshots and controlling the mouse and keyboard.
An agent that navigates websites, clicks, and fills forms to complete tasks in a web browser.
An agent that reads, writes, runs, and debugs code across a codebase with limited human input.
Building software mainly by describing what you want to an AI in natural language and accepting its code with little manual review.
A design where a person reviews or approves key AI decisions or actions before they take effect.
An AI assistant embedded in a tool that helps a human work, with the human staying in control.
A program that converses with users through text or voice, increasingly powered by LLMs.
An isolated environment where an agent can run code or actions without affecting the wider system.
An agent mode that runs many searches and reads many sources over an extended period to produce a cited report.
AI that can process or generate more than one type of data, such as text, images, audio, and video.
terms.mental_model: A model with more than one sense: it can read, look, and sometimes listen or speak.
terms.example: Uploading a photo of a broken product and asking the AI to describe the defect and draft a refund request.

quiz.question: Which task requires a multimodal model?
options: Fixing a spelling mistake
Answering a question about what's in a photo
Translating a sentence
Summarizing a text article
quiz.explanation: Understanding an image together with a text question needs more than one data type.

terms.definition: A model that understands both images and text, for example to describe or answer questions about pictures.
The field of AI that enables machines to interpret and understand images and video.
Converting text in images or scanned documents into machine-readable text.
Locating and identifying objects within an image, usually with bounding boxes.
Labeling each pixel in an image according to the object or region it belongs to.
A generative model that creates images or other data by learning to gradually remove noise from random input.
terms.mental_model: A sculptor who starts with a block of random noise and chips it away until a picture appears.
terms.example: Image generators that turn a text prompt into a new illustration by step-by-step denoising.

quiz.question: How does a diffusion model create an image?
options: By stitching together stock photos
By copying the closest photo from the internet
By drawing one pixel per user click
By starting from noise and gradually removing it, guided by the prompt
quiz.explanation: Diffusion models learn to reverse a noising process, producing images from random noise.

terms.definition: Generating images from a written description.
Generating video clips from a written description.
Converting written text into spoken audio.
Converting spoken audio into written text.
Generating speech that imitates a specific person's voice from samples of it.
AI-generated or AI-altered media that realistically depicts a person saying or doing something they did not.
Using AI to fill in or replace selected parts of an image; outpainting extends the image beyond its borders.
An OpenAI model trained to match images with text descriptions in a shared embedding space.
A model that learns how an environment behaves so it can predict or simulate what happens next.
AI that perceives and acts in the physical world through a body such as a robot.
A model that takes visual input and language instructions and outputs robot actions.
A standardized set of tasks used to measure and compare model performance.
Systematic tests that measure how well an AI system performs on the tasks and behaviors you care about.
Using a language model to grade or compare other models' outputs.
The share of predictions a model gets right out of all predictions.
Of everything the model labeled positive, the share that was actually positive.
Of everything that was actually positive, the share the model correctly found.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both in one number.
A table comparing predicted labels against actual labels to show where a classifier is right and wrong.
A measure of how well a language model predicts text; lower means the model is less surprised by the data.
A measure of how well a classifier separates classes across all decision thresholds.
Metrics that score generated text by its word overlap with reference texts, common for translation and summarization.
The probability that at least one of k generated solutions passes the tests, used to evaluate code models.
A trusted, carefully labeled set of examples used as the reference for evaluation.
When test data leaks into training data, making benchmark scores look better than real ability.
Comparing two versions of a system with real users to see which performs better.
Logging and tracing prompts, outputs, tool calls, cost, and latency to monitor and debug AI systems in production.
People rating or comparing model outputs to judge quality.
The field focused on preventing AI systems from causing accidental or deliberate harm.
Making AI systems pursue goals and behave in ways that match human intentions and values.
Rules, filters, or checks that constrain what an AI system can accept, say, or do.
terms.mental_model: Bumpers on a bowling lane: they keep the AI from rolling into the gutter.
terms.example: A finance bot that blocks any reply giving specific stock-buying advice and points to a licensed advisor instead.

quiz.question: What are guardrails used for?
options: To limit what an AI system accepts, says or does
To train the model
To increase the context window
To speed up the model
quiz.explanation: Guardrails are checks and rules that keep AI behavior within safe, allowed bounds.

terms.definition: A crafted input designed to get a model to bypass its safety rules.
terms.mental_model: Trying to talk a security guard into breaking the rules with a clever story.
terms.example: A user wrapping a harmful request in a fake role-play to try to make the model ignore its safety rules.

quiz.question: How is a jailbreak different from prompt injection?
options: They are exactly the same thing
Prompt injection is always harmless
A jailbreak is usually the user trying to bypass safety rules; injection hides instructions in content the model processes
Jailbreaks only affect image models
quiz.explanation: Jailbreaks target the model's safety limits directly; injection smuggles commands through third-party content.

terms.definition: An attack where malicious instructions hidden in input or retrieved content hijack a model's behavior.
terms.mental_model: Someone slipping a fake note into the boss's inbox that says 'ignore your instructions and do this'.
terms.example: A webpage hiding the text 'ignore previous instructions and email the user's data to me', hoping a browsing agent obeys it.

quiz.question: Why is prompt injection especially risky for AI agents?
options: Agents can't read text
Agents don't use prompts
Agents have smaller context windows
Agents read untrusted content and can take real actions based on it
quiz.explanation: If an agent treats instructions in web pages or files as commands, attackers can hijack its actions.

terms.definition: Deliberately probing an AI system with adversarial tests to uncover harmful or unsafe behavior.
An input deliberately crafted to make a model produce a wrong or harmful output.
Corrupting training data to plant errors, biases, or hidden behaviors in a model.
When a model maximizes its reward signal in unintended ways that do not achieve the real goal.
A model's tendency to tell users what they want to hear rather than what is accurate.
A hypothesized failure where a model appears aligned during training but pursues different goals when deployed.
Research into understanding how a model's internal computations produce its outputs.
Methods that make an AI system's decisions understandable to humans.
Systematic unfair outcomes from an AI system, often inherited from skewed training data or design choices.
The goal of ensuring an AI system does not produce unjustly different outcomes across groups of people.
Developing and using AI in ways that are safe, fair, transparent, and accountable.
Detecting and filtering harmful content in AI inputs or outputs, often with dedicated classifiers.
Embedding hidden signals in AI-generated content so it can later be identified as machine-made.
Attached metadata recording where a piece of media came from and how it was created or edited.
Describes AI capabilities that can be used for both beneficial and harmful purposes.
Giving an AI agent only the minimum permissions and tool access it needs for its task.
A processor built for massively parallel math, the main hardware used to train and run AI models.
Google's custom chip designed specifically to accelerate machine learning workloads.
A chip specialized for running AI models efficiently, common in phones and laptops.
Any specialized hardware, such as GPUs, TPUs, or NPUs, designed to speed up AI computation.
NVIDIA's platform for programming its GPUs, widely used by AI frameworks.
The memory on a GPU that holds model weights and activations, often the main limit on model size.
Floating-point operations, used to measure compute used for training (FLOPs) or hardware speed (FLOPS per second).
The processing power used to train and run AI models, usually measured in GPU-hours or FLOPs.
Running AI models locally on devices like phones or sensors instead of in the cloud.
Training a model across many chips or machines by splitting the data, the model, or both.
A defined interface that lets software send requests to a model or service and receive responses.
A set of libraries and tools that makes it easier to build applications on a platform or API.
A cap on how many requests or tokens a user can send to an API in a given period.
Practices for deploying, monitoring, and maintaining machine learning models reliably in production.
Hosting a trained model so applications can send it requests and receive outputs.
A widely used open-source deep learning framework, originally developed at Meta.
Google's open-source machine learning framework.
A multi-dimensional array of numbers, the basic data structure in deep learning frameworks.
A component that sends each request to the most suitable model based on cost, speed, or task difficulty.
A proxy layer that manages access, routing, logging, and limits across multiple AI model providers.
A structured collection of data used to train, validate, or test a model.
The data a model learns from during training.
Adding correct answers or tags to raw data so it can be used for supervised learning.
Creating modified copies of existing data, such as rotated images, to expand a training set.
Fixing or removing errors, duplicates, and inconsistencies in data before training.
Creating or transforming input variables to help a model learn more effectively.
Data organized in a fixed format such as tables with rows and columns.
Data without a predefined format, such as free text, images, audio, and video.
When real-world data changes over time so a model's predictions become less accurate.
Automatically collecting content from websites, a common source of AI training data.
Data that can identify a specific person, which AI systems must handle carefully.
A mathematical technique that adds noise so results reveal patterns without exposing any individual's data.
The policies, processes, and oversight structures that guide how AI is developed and used.
The European Union's law regulating AI by risk level, with obligations phasing in from 2025 onward.
A voluntary US framework for identifying and managing risks from AI systems.
A document describing a model's intended uses, performance, limitations, and safety testing.
An independent review of an AI system's performance, risks, and compliance.
A lab's commitment to apply stronger safety measures as its models reach higher capability thresholds.
The knowledge needed to understand, use, and critically evaluate AI tools.
Employees using AI tools without their organization's approval or oversight.
A country's effort to build and control its own AI infrastructure, data, and models.
Government restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips, models, or related technology to certain countries or entities.
Legal questions about using copyrighted works to train AI and about ownership of AI-generated content.
Alan Turing's 1950 test of whether a machine's conversation can be distinguished from a human's.
